text:
Parked on oak benches, in the corners
of the church that warms its breath, their eyes
fixed on the gilded choir, while the choir
roars pious songs from their throats,
inhaling wax like the smell of a loaf,
happy, humiliated, like beaten dogs,
the Good Lord's poor, the patron and master,
offer their Oremuses, ridiculous and obtuse.


It is fine to offer smooth benches to the female
after the six days in which God mistreats her!
for she rocks, wrapped in strange furs,
something akin to a child that cries without cease.


With filthy breasts in the open air, these soup women,
with prayer clinging to eyes that do not pray,
look at the little hussies with their sad display,
seekers beneath the brim of the deformed hat.


Outside, the cold and hunger and the man with his revelry:
well, then! one hour more; afterward, a thousand ills.
—Meanwhile, all around them, a little group of old women
with enormous double chins moans, drones, chatters.


And there are the epileptics and those terrified ones
whom everyone flees at the crossroads;
and, happily sniffing old missals,
those blind men whom a dog leads into the courtyards.


Drooling a beggarly and stupid faith,
they all tell their endless complaint to Jesus,
who dreams above, pallid in the yellow light,
far from thin sinners and potbellied sinners,


from the smell of flesh and moldy cloth:
humble, gloomy farce of disgusting gestures.
—And prayer blooms with chosen phrases,
and mysticism takes on urgent shades,


when the sun dies in the nave, and bland folds of silk,
dull green laughter, the ladies of distinguished neighborhoods,
—Jesus!—the liver-sick women,
offer their fingers to be kissed in the holy water.

translation.title: The Poor in Church
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Rimbaud's French original. The harsh social register and bodily grotesquerie are retained; the source's odd 'comacas' comparison is rendered as the clear little-dog image without importing a different scene.
